hook
If this tiny tail rotor stops, the whole helicopter spins out of control. Why? And how does a helicopter even fly?
blade
The main rotor blades are actually wings. They're curved and tilted, so as they spin, they push air downward.
lift
Push air down, and the air pushes the helicopter up. That's lift. Tilt the blades more, and it climbs.
torque
But here's the problem. When the engine spins the rotor one way, Newton's third law spins the body the other way.
tail
That's the tail rotor's job. It pushes air sideways, creating a force that cancels the spin and keeps the nose pointing straight.
yaw
Change how hard the tail rotor pushes, and the pilot can turn left or right, right on the spot.
tilt
To fly forward, the whole spinning rotor tilts. Now some of the lift pulls forward, and off it goes.
swash
This is done by a clever part called the swashplate. It changes each blade's angle as it spins around.
hover
And when the lift exactly matches the weight, the helicopter hovers perfectly still in the air.
twin
Some helicopters skip the tail rotor completely. They use two rotors spinning in opposite directions, so the spins cancel out!
outro
Spinning wings and a balancing tail. That's how a helicopter flies! Follow for more science made simple.
